title: The meat question
hook: Sikhs hold different views on eating meat; the code forbids ritually slaughtered meat only

segments.voice: Yesterday, open questions: the Ragmala, the calendar, and two cups of tea kept full during an argument. Your line was questions held kindly. Did you ask before you answered? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-three.

A family birthday, buffet style. Two cousins in line, both with a steel kara on the wrist, both wearing a turban. One fills a plate with dal, rice and paneer. The other adds a piece of tandoori chicken. Neither comments. An aunt watching from the end of the table has opinions, and keeps them for later. Ask Sikhs whether a Sikh can eat meat and the answers differ, sometimes inside one household. Today is that question, and what the Sikh code actually says.
screen: `TWO COUSINS, ONE BUFFET.` → `DAL ON ONE PLATE, CHICKEN ON ONE.` → `WHAT DOES THE CODE SAY?`

segments.voice: Start with the code. The Sikh Rehat Maryada lists a few things an initiated Sikh must never do. One of them is eating kutha, meat from an animal killed by ritual slaughter. Its readers notice what the line doesn't say: it doesn't forbid all meat. So some Sikhs eat meat killed with a single quick stroke, called jhatka, and see no conflict. Others read the whole spirit of Gurbani as pointing away from killing for food, and keep a vegetarian life. Some streams met earlier in this block, like the Namdharis, keep a vegetarian kitchen as a community. And the langar, the free kitchen, is traditionally vegetarian, so anyone of any diet can sit and eat the same meal. Now the Granth. In a passage on Ang 1289, Guru Nanak turns to people quarreling over flesh. Here in paraphrase: fools argue about meat, yet know nothing of spiritual wisdom or meditation. Readers hear that line in different ways. Some hear the Guru saying the argument itself misses the point. Others notice the passage goes on to observe that people are born of flesh, and read it as cutting through purity rules. Elsewhere, near the end of the Granth, couplets of Kabir speak sharply against killing, and some vegetarian Sikhs turn to them. So both sides open the same book. What they share is the line the code draws: no ritual slaughter, and a langar where every plate can be the same.
screen: `THE CODE: NO RITUALLY KILLED MEAT.` · `JHATKA FOR SOME, NO MEAT FOR OTHERS.` · `FOOLS ARGUE ABOUT FLESH.` · `BOTH SIDES OPEN THE SAME BOOK.` · then, large: `A LANGAR WHERE EVERY PLATE MATCHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a different diet. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person whose plate looks different from yours. A vegetarian friend, a cousin who fasts, a coworker who keeps a rule you don't. Picture sitting across from them at one table. Notice any small urge to comment, and let it go out with the breath. Then think of one thing you could cook or order that you could both share. If you pray, you can hold that table before Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The meat question. Sikhs differ on eating meat; the code draws its line at ritually slaughtered meat, and the langar keeps one vegetarian table for all. Today's word.
Your line: different plates. Today, at one meal, let someone else's plate be their own business, and if you can, choose one dish you could both eat. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs follow different diets: the Rehat Maryada forbids initiated Sikhs to eat kutha, ritually slaughtered meat; some Sikhs eat jhatka meat, others are vegetarian, and the langar is traditionally vegetarian so that all can share it.

fork.setup: you're Guru Nanak, and people are quarreling over whether meat is pure. what do you say?
options: fools argue about flesh, and know nothing of wisdom or meditation.
eat whatever you like; nothing matters.
fork.reveal: on Ang 1289 he turns the argument back on the arguers. readers still differ on what that means for the plate.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikhs are all vegetarian, or all meat-eaters.
what it means: Sikhs differ; the code forbids kutha, ritually slaughtered meat, and the langar stays vegetarian.
what a scholar hears: on Ang 1289 Guru Nanak calls the quarrel over flesh foolish, and readers on both sides cite that same passage.

notes: Ang 1289 'maas maas kar moorakh jhagre, giaan dhiaan nahi jaanai' paraphrased as 'fools argue about meat, yet know nothing of spiritual wisdom or meditation'; the following lines on being born of flesh summarized. Please confirm Ang and paraphrase.
Kabir's couplets against killing placed 'near the end of the Granth' (Salok Kabir, around Ang 1374–1377) without an exact Ang. Please confirm.

Rehat Maryada: eating kutha listed among the prohibitions for amritdhari Sikhs; definition given as meat from an animal killed by ritual slaughter. Please confirm wording, and whether naming its usual association with halal slaughter is better left out as here.
Namdharis described as keeping a vegetarian kitchen as a community; langar described as 'traditionally vegetarian'. Please confirm.
Some groups (e.g. the Akhand Kirtani Jatha, Damdami Taksal) teach vegetarianism for initiated Sikhs; not named here. Keeper to decide whether to add.
Editor: kutha now glossed as meat from ritual slaughter (cut 'slow', an unsourced and unfair gloss on another tradition's practice); 'vegetarian Sikhs often turn to' Kabir softened to 'some'.
